claim: Dietary magnesium (Mg2+) supplementation can enhance memory in young and aged rats.
source: Dietary magnesium (Mg2+) supplementation can enhance memory in young and aged rats.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Memory-enhancing capacity of dietary magnesium was largely ascribed to increases in hippocampal synaptic density and elevated expression of the NR2B subunit of the NMDA-type glutamate receptor.
source: Memory-enhancing capacity was largely ascribed to increases in hippocampal synaptic density and elevated expression of the NR2B subunit of the NMDA-type glutamate receptor.
evidence: This claim is based on prior research findings cited in the manuscript.

claim: Mg2+ feeding enhances long-term memory in Drosophila.
source: Here we show that Mg2+ feeding also enhances long-term memory in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1.

claim: Normal and Mg2+-enhanced fly memory appears independent of NMDA receptors in the mushroom body.
source: Normal and Mg2+-enhanced fly memory appears independent of NMDA receptors in the mushroom body
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Normal and Mg2+-enhanced fly memory requires expression of a conserved CNNM-type Mg2+-efflux transporter encoded by the unextended (uex) gene.
source: Normal and Mg2+-enhanced fly memory appears independent of NMDA receptors in the mushroom body and instead requires expression of a conserved CNNM-type Mg2+-efflux transporter encoded by the unextended (uex) gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing memory defects in uex mutants and rescue experiments presented in Figures 2-4.

claim: UEX contains a putative cyclic nucleotide-binding homology domain.
source: UEX contains a putative cyclic nucleotide-binding homology domain
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and structural predictions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutation of the UEX cyclic nucleotide-binding homology domain separates a vital role for uex from a function in memory.
source: its mutation separates a vital role for uex from a function in memory
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the uexT626NRR mutant shown in Figure 6.

claim: UEX localization in mushroom body Kenyon cells is altered in memory-defective flies harboring mutations in cAMP-related genes.
source: Moreover, UEX localization in mushroom body Kenyon cells (KCs) is altered in memory-defective flies harboring mutations in cAMP-related genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data in rut and dnc mutants shown in Figure 7.

claim: UEX-dependent efflux is required for slow rhythmic maintenance of KC Mg2+.
source: Functional imaging suggests that UEX-dependent efflux is required for slow rhythmic maintenance of KC Mg2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional imaging data using MagIC shown in Figure 8.

claim: Regulated neuronal Mg2+ efflux is critical for normal and Mg2+-enhanced memory.
source: We propose that regulated neuronal Mg2+ efflux is critical for normal and Mg2+-enhanced memory.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Magnesium (Mg2+) plays a critical role in cellular metabolism and is considered to be an essential co-factor for more than 350 enzymes.
source: Magnesium (Mg2+) plays a critical role in cellular metabolism and is considered to be an essential co-factor for more than 350 enzymes (Romani and Scarpa, 2000; Vink and Nechifor, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Alterations of Mg2+ homeostasis are associated with a broad range of clinical conditions affecting the nervous system.
source: As a result, alterations of Mg2+ homeostasis are associated with a broad range of clinical conditions, including those affecting the nervous system, such as glaucoma (DeToma et al., 2014), Parkinson's disease (Hermosura et al., 2005; Hermosura and Garruto, 2007; Lin et al., 2014; Shindo et al., 2016), Alzheimer's disease (Andrási et al., 2000; Andrási et al., 2005; Cilliler et al., 2007; Durlach et al., 1997; Glick, 1990; Lemke, 1995; Chui et al., 2011; Vural et al., 2010), anxiety (Sartori et al., 2012), depression (Whittle et al., 2011; Murck, 2002; Murck, 2013; Rasmussen et al., 1990; Ghafari et al., 2015), and intellectual disability (Arjona et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Increasing brain Mg2+ through diet can enhance neuronal plasticity and memory performance of young and aged rodents.
source: Perhaps surprisingly, increasing brain Mg2+ through diet can enhance neuronal plasticity and memory performance of young and aged rodents, measured in a variety of behavioral tasks (Slutsky et al., 2010; Landfield and Morgan, 1984; Mickley et al., 2013; Abumaria et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Elevated Mg2+ reduced cognitive deficits in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease.
source: In addition, elevated Mg2+ reduced cognitive deficits in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease (Li et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior research study.

claim: Elevated Mg2+ enhanced the extinction of fear memories.
source: and enhanced the extinction of fear memories (Abumaria et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior research study.

claim: Dietary Mg2+ may have therapeutic value for patients with a variety of memory-related problems.
source: These apparently beneficial effects have led to the proposal that dietary Mg2+ may have therapeutic value for patients with a variety of memory-related problems (Billard, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal cited from prior literature.

claim: The memory-enhancing property of Mg2+ in rodents has largely been attributed to increases in hippocampal synaptic density and the activity of N-methyl-D-aspartate glutamate receptors (NMDARs).
source: Despite the large number of potential sites of Mg2+ action in the brain, the memory-enhancing property in rodents has largely been attributed to increases in hippocampal synaptic density and the activity of N-methyl-D-aspartate glutamate receptors (NMDARs).
evidence: This claim is based on prior research findings cited in the manuscript.

claim: Extracellular Mg2+ blocks the channel pore of the NMDAR and thereby inhibits the passage of other ions.
source: Extracellular Mg2+ blocks the channel pore of the NMDAR and thereby inhibits the passage of other ions (Mayer et al., 1984; Bekkers and Stevens, 1993; Jahr and Stevens, 1990; Nowak et al., 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Prior neuronal depolarization is required to release the Mg2+ block on the NMDAR and permit glutamate-gated Ca2+ influx.
source: Importantly, prior neuronal depolarization, driven by other transmitter receptors, is required to release the Mg2+ block on the NMDAR and permit glutamate-gated Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about NMDAR function.

claim: The NMDAR plays an important role in neuronal plasticity as a potential Hebbian coincidence detector.
source: The NMDAR therefore plays an important role in neuronal plasticity as a potential Hebbian coincidence detector.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about NMDAR function.

claim: Acute elevation of extracellular Mg2+ concentration within the physiological range can antagonize induction of NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation.
source: Acute elevation of extracellular Mg2+ concentration ([Mg2+]e) within the physiological range (0.8–1.2 mM) can antagonize induction of NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation (Dunwiddie and Lynch, 1979; Malenka et al., 1992; Malenka and Nicoll, 1993; Slutsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Increasing extracellular Mg2+ for several hours in neuronal cultures leads to enhancement of NMDAR mediated currents and facilitation of the expression of LTP.
source: In contrast, increasing [Mg2+]e for several hours in neuronal cultures leads to enhancement of NMDAR mediated currents and facilitation of the expression of LTP (Slutsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior research study.

claim: The enhancing effects of increased extracellular Mg2+ were observed in vivo in the brain of rats fed with Mg2+-L-threonate.
source: The enhancing effects of increased [Mg2+]e were also observed in vivo in the brain of rats fed with Mg2+-L-threonate (Slutsky et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior research study.

claim: Hippocampal neuronal circuits undergo homeostatic plasticity to accommodate the increased extracellular Mg2+ by upregulating expression of NR2B subunit containing NMDARs.
source: Hippocampal neuronal circuits undergo homeostatic plasticity (Turrigiano, 2008) to accommodate the increased [Mg2+]e by upregulating expression of NR2B subunit containing NMDARs (Slutsky et al., 2004; Slutsky et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: The higher density of hippocampal synapses with NR2B containing NMDARs are believed to compensate for the chronic increase in extracellular Mg2+ by enhancing NMDAR currents during burst firing.
source: The higher density of hippocampal synapses with NR2B containing NMDARs are believed to compensate for the chronic increase in [Mg2+]e by enhancing NMDAR currents during burst firing.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior research findings.

claim: Mice that are genetically engineered to overexpress NR2B exhibit enhanced hippocampal LTP and behavioral memory.
source: In support of this model, mice that are genetically engineered to overexpress NR2B exhibit enhanced hippocampal LTP and behavioral memory (Tang et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior research study.

claim: Olfactory memory in Drosophila involves a heterosynaptic mechanism driven by reinforcing dopaminergic neurons, which results in presynaptic depression of cholinergic connections between odor-activated mushroom body Kenyon cells and downstream mushroom body output neurons.
source: Olfactory memory in Drosophila involves a heterosynaptic mechanism driven by reinforcing dopaminergic neurons, which results in presynaptic depression of cholinergic connections between odor-activated mushroom body (MB) Kenyon cells (KCs) and downstream mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) (Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Aso et al., 2010; Aso et al., 2012; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012; Plaçais et al., 2013; Owald et al., 2015; Hige et al., 2015; Barnstedt et al., 2016; Perisse et al., 2016; Aso et al., 2014; Owald and Waddell, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Olfactory information is conveyed to Kenyon cells by cholinergic transmission from olfactory projection neurons.
source: In addition, olfactory information is conveyed to KCs by cholinergic transmission from olfactory projection neurons (Yasuyama et al., 2002; Leiss et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: There is currently no obvious location for NMDAR-dependent plasticity in the known architecture of the cholinergic input or output layers of the Drosophila mushroom body.
source: Although it is conceivable that glutamate is delivered to the MB network via an as yet to be identified route, there is currently no obvious location for NMDAR-dependent plasticity in the known architecture of the cholinergic input or output layers (Barnstedt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on current knowledge of mushroom body architecture.

claim: The fly provides a potential model to investigate other mechanisms through which dietary Mg2+ might enhance memory.
source: The fly therefore provides a potential model to investigate other mechanisms through which dietary Mg2+ might enhance memory.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the utility of the fly model.

claim: The reinforcing effects of dopamine depend on the Dop1R D1-type dopamine receptor.
source: The reinforcing effects of dopamine depend on the Dop1R D1-type dopamine receptor (Kim et al., 2007; Qin et al., 2012; Handler et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: The Dop1R D1-type dopamine receptor is positively coupled with cAMP production.
source: which is positively coupled with cAMP production (Tomchik and Davis, 2009; Boto et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: The dunce and rutabaga encoded cAMP phosphodiesterase and type I Ca2+-stimulated adenylate cyclase, respectively, are essential for olfactory memory in Drosophila.
source: Moreover, early studies in Drosophila identified the dunce and rutabaga encoded cAMP phosphodiesterase and type I Ca2+-stimulated adenylate cyclase, respectively, to be essential for olfactory memory (Dudai et al., 1976; Byers et al., 1981; Dudai and Zvi, 1984; Chen et al., 1986; Livingstone et al., 1984; Levin et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Hormones or agents that increase cellular cAMP level often elicit a significant Na+-dependent extrusion of Mg2+ into the extracellular space in mammalian cells.
source: Studies in mammalian cells have shown that hormones or agents that increase cellular cAMP level often elicit a significant Na+-dependent extrusion of Mg2+ into the extracellular space (Romani and Scarpa, 1990b; Romani and Scarpa, 1990a; Romani and Scarpa, 2000; Vink and Nechifor, 2011; Vormann and Günther, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: It is unclear whether Mg2+ extrusion plays any role in memory processing.
source: However, it is unclear whether Mg2+ extrusion plays any role in memory processing.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Wild-type flies fed for 4 days before training with food supplemented with 80 mM MgCl2 exhibited significantly enhanced 24 hr memory performance.
source: Surprisingly, wild-type flies fed for 4 days before training with food supplemented with additional magnesium chloride (MgCl2) exhibited significantly enhanced 24 hr memory performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Memory enhancement by dietary Mg2+ depends on concentration and was maximal when food was supplemented with 80 mM MgCl2.
source: Memory enhancement depends on concentration and was maximal when food was supplemented with 80 mM MgCl2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Immediate memory performance was not obviously enhanced by dietary Mg2+ supplementation.
source: Immediate memory performance was not obviously enhanced (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The enhancing effect of MgCl2 was also observed in flies fed with magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) but not calcium chloride (CaCl2).
source: The enhancing effect of MgCl2 was also observed in flies fed with magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) but not calcium chloride (CaCl2) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The memory enhancing effects can be specifically attributed to dietary supplementation of divalent Mg2+.
source: The memory enhancing effects can therefore be specifically attributed to dietary supplementation of divalent Mg2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of the effect to Mg2+ salts.

claim: RT-qPCR analyses did not reveal a significant difference in the abundance of mRNAs for glutamate receptors in heads taken from flies fed with 80 mM MgCl2 versus those fed with 1 mM MgCl2.
source: RT-qPCR analyses did not reveal a significant difference in the abundance of mRNAs for the putative NMDA (Nmdar1, Nmdar2), AMPA (GluRIA), or kainate-type (GluRIIA) receptors in heads taken from flies fed for 4 days with 80 mM MgCl2 versus those fed with 1 mM MgCl2 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Flies expressing Nmdar1RNAi in αβ neurons retained robust Mg2+-enhanced memory.
source: Moreover, flies expressing Nmdar1RNAi in αβ neurons retained robust Mg2+-enhanced memory (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mg2+-enhanced memory does not require NMDAR function in αβ KCs.
source: These results suggest that Mg2+-enhanced memory does not alter expression of glutamate receptors, or require NMDAR function in αβ KCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: The MagFRET signal was significantly higher in both the α and β collaterals of αβ KCs of flies fed with 80 mM than in those fed with 1 mM MgCl2.
source: The MagFRET signal was significantly higher in both the α and β collaterals of αβ KCs of flies fed with 80 mM, than in those fed with 1 mM (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by MagFRET imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mg2+ feeding elevates neuronal intracellular Mg2+ concentration.
source: This result indicates that Mg feeding elevates neuronal [Mg2+]i.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MagFRET measurements.

claim: The ~8% enhancement of the MagFRET signal measured in flies fed 80 mM MgCl2 corresponds approximately to a 50 µM increase of αβ KC intracellular Mg2+ on average.
source: Given the affinity of MagFRET-1 (Kd = 148 µM) and the ~50% increase in FRET signal upon Mg2+ binding (Lindenburg et al., 2013), we estimate that the ~8% enhancement of the MagFRET signal measured in flies fed 80 mM MgCl2 corresponds approximately to a 50 µM increase of αβ KC [Mg2+]i on average.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of MagFRET-1 and the measured signal change.

claim: Flies with the uexMI01943 MiMIC insertion showed a strong defect in 24 hr memory, but their performance immediately after training was indistinguishable from that of wild-type controls.
source: Flies with the uexMI01943 MiMIC insertion (Venken et al., 2011) showed a strong defect in 24 hr memory, but their performance immediately after training was indistinguishable from that of wild-type controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: More detailed analysis of uexMI01943 flies revealed a steady decay of memory that first became significantly different to that of wild-type flies 12 hr after training.
source: More detailed analysis of uexMI01943 flies revealed a steady decay of memory that first became significantly different to that of wild-type flies 12 hr after training (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No memory defect was evident in heterozygous uexMI01943/+ flies, demonstrating that this putative uex allele is recessive.
source: No memory defect was evident in heterozygous uexMI01943/+ flies, demonstrating that this putative uex allele is recessive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: UEX is the single fly ortholog of the four human CNNM genes that encode Mg2+ transporters.
source: uex piqued our attention because it is the single fly ortholog of the four human CNNM genes that encode Mg2+ transporters (Ishii et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research and sequence analysis.

claim: UEX contains a putative cyclic nucleotide-binding homology domain that is structurally related to those in cyclic nucleotide-gated channels.
source: and it also contains a putative CNBH domain that is structurally related to those in cyclic nucleotide-gated channels (Zagotta et al., 2003; Flynn et al., 2007; Kesters et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and structural analysis.

claim: Alignment of the 834 amino acid UEX sequence with CNNM1-4 reveals particularly high sequence conservation with CNNM2 and CNNM4 in the DUF21, CBS pair, and CNBH domains.
source: Alignment of the 834 amino acid UEX sequence with CNNM1-4 reveals particularly high sequence conservation with CNNM2 and CNNM4 in the DUF21, CBS pair, and CNBH domains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: MiMIC removal in uexMI01943.ex1 and uexMI01943.ex2 flies restored normal 24 hr memory performance, demonstrating that the MiMIC insertion is required for the uexMI01943 memory defect.
source: MiMIC removal in uexMI01943.ex1 and uexMI01943.ex2 flies restored normal 24 hr memory performance, demonstrating that the MiMIC insertion is required for the uexMI01943 memory defect (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Flies homozygous for the uexΔ mutation were not viable as adults, dying at the larval stage.
source: Flies homozygous for the resulting uexΔ mutation were not viable as adults, dying at the larval stage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation.

claim: Heterozygous uexMI01943/uexΔ flies were viable, but their 24 hr appetitive memory was significantly impaired.
source: In contrast, heterozygous uexMI01943/uexΔ flies were viable, but their 24 hr appetitive memory was significantly impaired (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: uex is an essential gene.
source: These data demonstrate that uex is an essential gene
evidence: This is an inference based on the lethality of the uexΔ homozygous mutation.

claim: uexMI01943 is a viable hypomorphic allele of uex.
source: and that uexMI01943 is a viable hypomorphic allele of uex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic complementation test.

claim: Homozygous uexMI01943 flies exhibited immediate aversive memory that was indistinguishable from that of heterozygous and wild-type controls.
source: Homozygous uexMI01943 flies exhibited immediate memory that was indistinguishable from that of heterozygous and wild-type controls (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The 24 hr aversive memory of homozygous uexMI01943 flies, formed following either five trials of aversive spaced training or one trial of fasting facilitated training, was significantly impaired.
source: However, their 24 hr memory, formed following either five trials of aversive spaced training (Tully et al., 1994; Jacob and Waddell, 2020), or one trial of fasting facilitated training (Hirano et al., 2013), was significantly impaired (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: uexMI01943 flies are more generally compromised in their ability to form LTM.
source: These experiments suggest that uexMI01943 flies are more generally compromised in their ability to form LTM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the defects observed in both appetitive and aversive LTM.

claim: VT23256-driven UAS-EGFP revealed restricted expression in αβ KCs with particularly strong label in αβc neurons.
source: VT23256-driven UAS-EGFP revealed restricted expression in αβ KCs with particularly strong label in αβ core (αβc) neurons (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Immunostaining flies harboring the uex::HA locus with an anti-HA antibody revealed prominent labeling of all the major KC classes in the MB, in addition to lower expression throughout the brain.
source: Immunostaining flies harboring this uex::HA locus with an anti-HA antibody revealed prominent labeling of all the major KC classes in the MB, in addition to lower expression throughout the brain (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Flies expressing uexRNAi in all αβ KCs or only in αβc KCs showed normal immediate memory but significantly impaired 24 hr memory.
source: Flies expressing uexRNAi (Perkins et al., 2015) in all αβ KCs (c739-GAL4; Yang et al., 1995; Perisse et al., 2013) or only in αβc KCs (NP7175-GAL4; Tanaka et al., 2008) showed normal immediate memory but significantly impaired 24 hr memory (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: uexRNAi expression in αβs or α′β′ KCs did not significantly alter immediate or LTM performance.
source: In contrast, uexRNAi expression in αβ surface (αβs, 0770-GAL4; Perisse et al., 2013) or α′β′ KCs (c305a-GAL4; Krashes et al., 2007) did not significantly alter immediate or LTM performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Normal 24 hr appetitive memory performance is particularly sensitive to uex expression in αβc neurons.
source: Normal 24 hr appetitive memory performance is therefore particularly sensitive to uex expression in αβc neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: Restricting UAS-uexRNAi expression to αβ KCs in adult flies using c739-GAL4 with GAL80ts produced a similar 24 hr specific memory defect to that observed when UAS-uexRNAi was expressed without temporal control.
source: Restricting UAS-uexRNAi expression to αβ KCs in adult flies using c739-GAL4 with GAL80ts produced a similar 24 hr specific memory defect to that observed when UAS-uexRNAi was expressed without temporal control (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: uexRNAi expression significantly reduced anti-HA signal in the αβ and γ KCs.
source: Comparing the intensity of immunolabeling in brains from uex::HA; MB247-GAL4/uexRNAi flies with that from uex::HA; MB247-GAL4/+ flies showed that uexRNAi expression significantly reduced anti-HA signal in the αβ and γ KCs (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Memory performance of uexMI01943 flies expressing UAS-uex in αβ and γ KCs or only the αβ KCs was significantly improved over that of uexMI01943 flies, and was statistically indistinguishable from that of controls with an intact uex locus.
source: Memory performance of uexMI01943 flies expressing UAS-uex in αβ and γ KCs (MB247-GAL4; Zars et al., 2000) or only the αβ KCs (c739-GAL4) was significantly improved over that of uexMI01943 flies, and was statistically indistinguishable from that of controls with an intact uex locus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: UAS-uex expression in α′β′, αβc, or αβs KCs did not restore memory performance to uexMI01943 flies.
source: In contrast, UAS-uex expression in α′β′, αβc, or αβs KCs did not restore memory performance to uexMI01943 flies
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Overexpressing uex in αβ KCs of wild-type flies did not augment 24 hr memory.
source: and overexpressing uex in αβ KCs of wild-type flies did not augment 24 hr memory (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Normal 24 hr memory performance could be restored to uexMI01943 flies if UAS-uex expression was confined to c739-GAL4 neurons in adulthood using GAL80ts-mediated temporal control.
source: Normal 24 hr memory performance could also be restored to uexMI01943 flies if UAS-uex expression was confined to c739-GAL4 neurons (all αβ KCs) in adulthood using GAL80ts-mediated temporal control (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: UEX plays an important role in adult αβ KCs.
source: Together, these loss-of-function RNAi and restoration experiments establish that UEX plays an important role in adult αβ KCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi and rescue experiments.

claim: UEX function in αβc KCs is essential for appetitive LTM, whereas both the αβc and αβs KCs need to have functional UEX to support LTM.
source: Finding that αβc RNAi knockdown of uex produces a memory defect (Figure 3C) but UAS-uex expression in αβc does not rescue the uexMI01943 mutant defect (Figure 4A) suggests that UEX function in αβc KCs is essential for appetitive LTM, whereas both the αβc and αβs KCs need to have functional UEX to support LTM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of RNAi and rescue results.

claim: The ability of UAS-uex to restore performance to uexMI0194 flies provides further support that uex is responsible for the memory impairment in uexMI01943 flies.
source: In addition, the ability of UAS-uex to restore performance to uexMI0194 flies provides further support that uex is responsible for the memory impairment in uexMI01943 flies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments.

claim: Flies carrying the uexMI01943 allele did not show enhanced memory when fed with 80 mM MgCl2, as compared to flies fed with 1 mM MgCl2.
source: Flies carrying the uexMI01943 allele (Figure 4F) or those expressing UAS-uexRNAi in the αβ KCs with c739-GAL4 (Figure 4E) did not show enhanced memory when fed with 80 mM MgCl2, as compared to flies fed with 1 mM MgCl2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The Mg2+-enhanced memory was recovered in uexMI01943 mutant flies when uex expression was restored to the αβ KCs.
source: Moreover, the Mg2+-enhanced memory was recovered in uexMI01943 mutant flies when uex expression was restored to the αβ KCs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: All control flies with unperturbed uex expression exhibited significantly enhanced memory when fed with 80 mM as compared to 1 mM MgCl2.
source: All control flies (c739-GAL4, UAS-uexRNAi, and UAS-uex) with unperturbed uex expression exhibited significantly enhanced memory when fed with 80 mM as compared to 1 mM MgCl2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Overexpressing UAS-uex in αβ KCs with c739-GAL4 in flies with a wild-type genetic background neither enhanced regular 24 hr memory, or that in flies fed for 4 days with 40 or 80 mM MgCl2.
source: Overexpressing UAS-uex in αβ KCs with c739-GAL4 in flies with a wild-type genetic background neither enhanced regular 24 hr memory (Figure 4B), or that in flies fed for 4 days with 40 or 80 mM MgCl2 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and G.

claim: Memory of wild-type, but not uexMI01943 mutant flies showed enhancement with 4 days of 80 mM MgCl2 supplementation following aversive spaced training.
source: Again, memory of wild-type, but not uexMI01943 mutant flies showed enhancement (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optimal memory enhancement with Mg2+ feeding requires, and can be fully supported by, UEX function in αβ KCs.
source: Together these results indicate that optimal memory enhancement with Mg2+ feeding requires, and can be fully supported by, UEX function in αβ KCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Mg2+ feeding experiments with uex mutants and rescue.

claim: Only expression of wild-type CNNM2, and not point-mutant forms, in αβ KCs of uexMI01943 mutant flies restored 24 hr memory performance.
source: However, only expression of wild-type CNNM2, and not point-mutant forms, in αβ KCs of uexMI01943 mutant flies restored 24 hr memory performance (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: UEX expressed in HEK293 cells localized to the plasma membrane and cells loaded with Mg2+ and the Mg2+ indicator Magnesium Green showed rapid Mg2+ efflux.
source: UEX expressed in HEK293 cells localized to the plasma membrane and cells loaded with Mg2+ and the Mg2+ indicator Magnesium Green showed rapid Mg2+ efflux (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 1.

claim: Mg2+ extrusion driven by UEX was noticeably less efficient than in cells expressing Human CNNM4.
source: Mg2+ extrusion driven by UEX was noticeably less efficient than in cells expressing Human CNNM4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Demonstration of cross-species complementation and Mg2+ efflux activity defines UEX as a functional homolog of mammalian CNNM2/4.
source: Nevertheless, demonstration of cross-species complementation and Mg2+ efflux activity defines UEX as a functional homolog of mammalian CNNM2/4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complementation and efflux experiments.
